chapterTitle: Functions, Events, and Basic Object Interaction

screens.title: Functions, Events, and Basic Object Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we bring three core ideas together: functions for organizing reusable code, UnityEvents for flexible, inspector-driven callbacks, and collision/trigger callbacks for object interaction. You'll learn what a function is, how parameters and return types work, and why extracting logic into named methods makes your project easier to extend. Then you'll see UnityEvent, a lightweight way to expose interaction hooks so designers can wire responses without changing code. Finally, we'll cover collision and trigger methods that Unity calls automatically when colliders meet, and practical ways scripts on different GameObjects obtain references to one another. Throughout, you will practice safe patterns such as null checks and inspector assignments so your game avoids common runtime errors. For example, a TakeDamage function centralizes damage logic, a UnityEvent called OnPlayerCollectedItem lets a level designer choose what happens when a pickup is collected, and OnTriggerEnter detects when the player steps into a healing area. By the end you should be able to define public methods, set up a UnityEvent in the Inspector, detect collisions or triggers correctly, and connect scripts across GameObjects while guarding against null references. Consider how a small, well-named function can save time when you duplicate behavior across enemies or items.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide your practice so you build reliable interactions. First, you will define and call custom C# functions with parameters and return types. That means you'll write named methods such as TakeDamage(int amount) or CalculateDistance that accept inputs and optionally return values. Second, you'll understand how functions support code reusability and modularity so you avoid repeating the same logic across scripts. Third, you'll set up UnityEvents to create flexible, designer-friendly callbacks in the Inspector. With UnityEvent, a level designer can wire a button or pickup to any public method without changing code. Fourth, you'll implement basic collision detection using OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter, and establish safe communication between scripts on different GameObjects, including performing null checks before calling another script's methods. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters in a real project, and you'll practice wiring these behaviors in the Inspector so runtime behavior is predictable and maintainable.

screens.title: Bloom's Taxonomy: Learn → Apply → Master
screens.narratorSegment: To make steady progress, follow a simple learning path. First, learn the syntax and structure of functions, UnityEvent, and the collision callbacks. Practice by writing simple methods and confirming they run. Next, apply those skills by wiring UnityEvent callbacks in the Inspector and by creating small interactions—like a pickup that heals the player via an event or an enemy that takes damage from a function call. Finally, master the patterns by combining them: create reusable damage functions, trigger events on collisions, and use safe script references with null checks and inspector-assigned objects. Along the way, test for common mistakes such as missing Rigidbody components or unassigned references. This progression helps you move from seeing code run to designing interactions that others on your team, such as level designers, can change without touching scripts.

screens.title: What is a Function (Method)?
screens.narratorSegment: A function, also called a method in C#, is a named block of code that performs a single task and can be called from other places in your scripts. It typically has a return type that says what it gives back after running or void if it returns nothing, a name that communicates purpose, and optionally parameters that accept inputs. For example, a TakeDamage function that accepts an integer amount centralizes health reduction so you never duplicate the logic in many places. A CalculateDistance function can accept two Vector3 positions and return a float distance. Writing functions makes code modular: you can change the logic in one place rather than hunting through many scripts. A common misconception is to think functions should always be short. While readability is important, functions should represent a single logical operation — complex behavior can be composed from smaller functions. This makes testing easier and reduces bugs. In practice, mark functions public when other scripts should call them, and keep utility methods private when they are internal helpers. Consider naming and parameter choices carefully so the function reads like a sentence when called.

keyIdea.title: Function essentials
keyIdea.text: Name, parameters, and return type form a function's contract. Use them to encapsulate and reuse behavior across your game.

content.html:
Definition › Function (Method)
Structure of a function
  • Return type: what the function yields (or void).
  • Name: describes what it does, e.g., TakeDamage.
  • Parameters: inputs that change behavior, e.g., int amount.
  • Body: the statements that execute when called.
Concrete example
TakeDamage(int amount): reduces player health, plays damage effect, and checks for death. Centralizing this avoids duplicate logic across enemy attacks.
Key Takeaway

Think of a function as a single, testable action with a clear name and inputs. It should do one thing well.

Analogy & common mistake
Analogy: A function is like a toolbox tool — you pick it by name and supply what it needs. Common mistake: copying and pasting the same block instead of creating a function, which leads to many places to update when logic changes.
Try this
  1. Find repeated code in your project.
  2. Extract it into a named method with parameters where needed.
  3. Replace duplicates with calls to the new method.

screens.title: Designing Reusable Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Turning repeated logic into a reusable function follows a small process. First, identify the repeated behavior: damage calculation, health clamping, or playing a sound. Second, list the varying inputs: the damage amount, the damage type, or a target GameObject. Third, design the function signature: choose a descriptive name, decide parameters and the return type if needed. Fourth, move the logic into the function body and replace each duplicate with a call. Finally, test all call sites to confirm behavior is unchanged. For example, TakeDamage(int amount) can accept an enum for damage type or return a bool indicating whether the entity died; those choices depend on how callers use the function. A frequent misconception is overloading every small behavior into a single function. Instead, prefer smaller functions that compose into larger behavior. Smaller functions are easier to unit test and reason about. Also document side effects, such as whether the function calls Destroy or triggers animations, so callers know the contract. The result is less duplication and fewer bugs when behavior changes. Designing Reusable Functions means identify repetition, extract parameters, design a clear signature, replace duplicates, and test. prefer composition over monolithic methods.. In practical terms, from repeated code to a single reusable method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor steps
keyIdea.text: Identify repetition, extract parameters, design a clear signature, replace duplicates, and test. Prefer composition over monolithic methods.

content.html:
Process › Refactoring to functions
Step-by-step
1. Identify repetition
Find blocks that appear in multiple scripts or methods.
2. Extract inputs
List parameters the logic needs, like an amount or a target.
3. Create signature
Choose visibility, name, parameters, and return type.
4. Replace calls and test
Call the new method from previous places and validate behavior.
Concrete example
Imagine several weapons reducing player health with similar code. Extract a public void TakeDamage(int amount) that reduces health, clamps it, and fires death when needed. Now every weapon calls TakeDamage, and death logic is maintained in one place.
Key Takeaway

Refactoring to functions reduces duplication and centralizes behavior, making changes safer and faster.

screens.title: UnityEvent: Designer-Friendly Callbacks
screens.narratorSegment: UnityEvent is a Unity system that lets you expose callback points in your scripts so any public method on a GameObject's component can be called when an event fires. You declare a UnityEvent field, for example public UnityEvent OnPlayerCollectedItem, and then call OnPlayerCollectedItem. Invoke() at the appropriate time in your script. In the Inspector, designers can drag GameObjects into the event and pick which public method to call, including methods with parameters that are allowed by UnityEvent. This decouples the code that triggers the event from the concrete objects that respond, which makes interaction wiring flexible and maintainable. A common misconception is to treat UnityEvent as a replacement for all code; instead, use it for designer-configurable connections while keeping important game logic in functions. Another practical tip is to include defensive checks or fallback behavior in case no listeners are assigned. Remember to include using UnityEngine. Events at the top of your C# file to access UnityEvent. In short, UnityEvent moves wiring from code into the Editor so the same trigger can invoke different effects across levels without changing scripts.

keyIdea.title: UnityEvent in one line
keyIdea.text: Declare a UnityEvent, expose it in the Inspector, and invoke it at runtime to call designer-assigned public methods without hard-coded references.

content.html:
Definition › UnityEvent
How it works
  • Declare public UnityEvent MyEvent; and include using UnityEngine.Events.
  • In the Inspector, bind GameObjects and select public methods to invoke.
  • Call MyEvent.Invoke() from code to trigger all bound methods.
Designer-friendly example
A collectible can fire OnPlayerCollectedItem.Invoke() so level designers decide whether it heals the player, plays a sound, or spawns a particle effect.
Best practices & pitfalls
Avoid using UnityEvent for every internal call. Use it where wiring in the Editor adds value. Also consider default behavior if no listeners are assigned and document the event's intent so designers know which methods to bind.
Pro Tip

Use UnityEvent for level-specific or designer-driven responses, and keep core game logic in functions you can call from listeners.

screens.title: Invoking UnityEvent and Inspector Wiring
screens.narratorSegment: To make a UnityEvent work end-to-end, follow a clear sequence. First, add using UnityEngine. Events at the top of your file and declare a public UnityEvent field. Second, in the Inspector, expand the event and use the plus button to add listeners: drag a GameObject into the slot and then choose a public method on one of its components. Third, ensure that the method you want to call is public and matches one of the accepted signatures UnityEvent supports. Fourth, in your script call MyEvent. Invoke() when the condition occurs, for example when the player picks up an item. Fifth, test the scene and confirm that the chosen methods run. A common error is forgetting to mark the method public or selecting a method with an incompatible signature in the Inspector. Also remember that UnityEvent creates coupling through the Editor: it's flexible, but you still need to ensure listeners exist or handle missing listeners gracefully. This flow lets designers reconfigure scene behavior without modifying code while programmers keep predictable control over when an event fires. Invoking UnityEvent and Inspector Wiring means declare the event, bind listeners in the inspector, ensure public methods are available, and call invoke() when appropriate. test with and without listeners.. In practical terms, from code declaration to runtime invocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event wiring checklist
keyIdea.text: Declare the event, bind listeners in the Inspector, ensure public methods are available, and call Invoke() when appropriate. Test with and without listeners.

content.html:
Process › Wiring UnityEvent
Step sequence
  1. Add using UnityEngine.Events and declare public UnityEvent.
  2. In Inspector, click + and drag GameObject to the listener slot.
  3. Select a public method on the component to call.
  4. Invoke the event in code when appropriate.
  5. Test both with listeners and with none assigned.
Scenario
A collectible invokes OnPlayerCollectedItem.Invoke(). The designer assigns the Player's Heal method in the Inspector so collecting triggers healing. Swap the listener later to play a sound instead without changing code.
Common Mistake

Forgetting to include the UnityEngine.Events namespace or selecting a non-public method will prevent the Inspector from listing expected methods.

screens.title: OnCollisionEnter vs OnTriggerEnter
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides two families of callbacks for interactions: OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter. OnCollisionEnter is used for physical collisions when colliders contact and at least one object has a Rigidbody; it supplies a Collision object with contact information. Use collisions when objects should bounce, push, or respond physically. OnTriggerEnter is used when a collider marked Is Trigger detects overlaps; this does not cause physical responses and is ideal for zones, pickups, or fields. Triggers require at least one Rigidbody on interacting objects as well. A common mistake is forgetting to add any Rigidbody: without at least one Rigidbody, neither method will fire. Another confusion is using a non-trigger collider when you want overlap detection — remember to check Is Trigger for zones. Both systems have Enter, Stay, and Exit variants to detect beginning, continuous presence, and leaving. Choose collisions for physics responses and triggers for event detection and pickups. Designing your colliders and rigidbodies correctly is the main setup step to get these callbacks to run reliably. OnCollisionEnter vs OnTriggerEnter means use oncollisionenter for physical contact and ontriggerenter for non-physical overlap detection. ensure rigidbody and collider settings match the intended behavior.. In practical terms, when to use collisions and when to use triggers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pick the right callback
keyIdea.text: Use OnCollisionEnter for physical contact and OnTriggerEnter for non-physical overlap detection. Ensure Rigidbody and collider settings match the intended behavior.

content.html:
Comparison › Collision vs Trigger
OnCollisionEnter
Called when colliders with appropriate Rigidbody setup physically collide. Receives a Collision parameter containing contact points, relative velocity, and the other GameObject.
Use when you need physics reactions such as bouncing, knocking back, or applying forces.
OnTriggerEnter
Called when a collider marked Is Trigger detects overlap with another collider; it receives a Collider parameter. No physical interaction is applied.
Use for pickups, areas that grant buffs or damage, and non-physical detection.
Setup checklist
Add collider(s)
Ensure at least one Rigidbody
Toggle Is Trigger for overlap-only behavior

screens.title: Rigidbody and Collider Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Correct collider and Rigidbody configuration is the most common source of confusion when collision callbacks don't fire. Remember these rules: at least one of the interacting GameObjects must have a Rigidbody for collision or trigger callbacks to run. Colliders must be enabled and not set to a disabled layer. For trigger behavior, check Is Trigger on the collider that should act as an overlap detector—either the zone or the pickup can be the trigger. A common beginner mistake is attaching a Rigidbody to every moving object without considering constraints; instead, add Rigidbody where physics or movement is required and use kinematic rigidbodies when you move objects directly via transform. Another pitfall is expecting OnTriggerEnter to run when both colliders are static (no Rigidbody present) — it will not. If callbacks are missing, check the console for warnings, ensure tags and layers are correct, and verify that colliders are not set to be ignored by collision matrices. These setup checks will save debugging time and prevent surprises when testing scenes. keyIdea.title: Setup rules
keyIdea.text: At least one Rigidbody is required. Use Is Trigger for overlap detection. Verify colliders are enabled and not excluded by collision layers.

content.html:
Definition › Rigidbody & Collider
Checklist to troubleshoot callbacks
  • Is at least one Rigidbody present on the interacting objects?
  • Are colliders enabled and sized correctly?
  • Is Is Trigger checked for overlap behavior?
  • Is the collision matrix preventing interaction between layers?
Practical tips
Use kinematic Rigidbody for objects moved by scripts to keep physics consistent. When debugging, temporarily color or scale colliders so you can see overlaps in scene view. Test trigger and collision behaviors separately to isolate issues.
Warning

If you forget Rigidbody or misconfigure Is Trigger, neither OnCollisionEnter nor OnTriggerEnter will fire as expected.

screens.title: Script Communication Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Scripts communicate by getting references to one another so they can call public methods or access data. There are several common methods: direct inspector references where a public field is assigned by dragging the target GameObject into the slot; GetComponent when the target component lives on the same GameObject; GetComponentInParent or GetComponentInChildren for family relationships; GameObject. Find or FindWithTag to search the scene by name or tag; and singletons for a globally accessible instance. Each has trade-offs. Inspector references are explicit and designer-friendly but require assignments. GetComponent is fast for same-object components. Find methods work but are slower and fragile if used frequently, especially every frame. Singletons are convenient for managers but introduce global coupling. Across all these approaches, perform null checks after attempting to obtain a reference. For example, if GetComponent returns null, log a clear warning and avoid invoking methods on the missing reference. Choosing the right pattern depends on ownership, lifetime, and whether designers need to reassign references in the Editor. Script Communication Patterns means prefer inspector assignment or getcomponent where appropriate; use find sparingly and singletons only when a global instance fits the design.. In practical terms, how scripts on different gameobjects find and call each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture › Script Communication

screens.title: Null Checks and Runtime Safety
screens.narratorSegment: NullReferenceException occurs when code tries to access a member on a null reference. In Unity this happens frequently when GetComponent, GameObject. Find, or inspector references are missing. The simple defensive pattern is to check for null after obtaining a reference and before calling methods or accessing fields. For example, if enemyAI = targetEnemy. GetComponent<EnemyAI>(); then check if (enemyAI!= null) before calling enemyAI. TakeDamage(10). If null, log a helpful warning indicating which GameObject and which script is missing. Null checks are not just defensive: they document assumptions about scene setup and make debugging faster. Remember to cache references in Awake or Start, not every frame, to avoid repeated searches. Core Safety › Null Checks
Why null checks matter
A single null call can stop gameplay and flood the console. Check references immediately after locating them and provide informative logs to speed debugging and improve team workflows.
Pattern

if (enemyAI != null) { enemyAI.TakeDamage(10); } else { Debug.LogWarning("EnemyAI missing on targetEnemy"); }

Fail fast vs graceful handling
For critical components, log an error in Awake so the problem is visible early. For optional systems, handle null gracefully and provide a fallback. Both approaches improve robustness.
Cache references in Awake or Start rather than calling Find or GetComponent repeatedly in Update. This keeps runtime performance stable.

In this chapter we bring three core ideas together: functions for organizing reusable code, UnityEvents for flexible, inspector-driven callbacks, and collision/trigger callbacks for object interaction. You'll learn what a function is, how parameters and return types work, and why extracting logic into named methods makes your project easier to extend. Then you'll see UnityEvent, a lightweight way to expose interaction hooks so designers can wire responses without changing code. Finally, we'll cover collision and trigger methods that Unity calls automatically when colliders meet, and practical ways scripts on different GameObjects obtain references to one another. Throughout, you will practice safe patterns such as null checks and inspector assignments so your game avoids common runtime errors. For example, a TakeDamage function centralizes damage logic, a UnityEvent called OnPlayerCollectedItem lets a level designer choose what happens when a pickup is collected, and OnTriggerEnter detects when the player steps into a healing area. By the end you should be able to define public methods, set up a UnityEvent in the Inspector, detect collisions or triggers correctly, and connect scripts across GameObjects while guarding against null references. Consider how a small, well-named function can save time when you duplicate behavior across enemies or items.

These objectives guide your practice so you build reliable interactions. First, you will define and call custom C# functions with parameters and return types. That means you'll write named methods such as TakeDamage(int amount) or CalculateDistance that accept inputs and optionally return values. Second, you'll understand how functions support code reusability and modularity so you avoid repeating the same logic across scripts. Third, you'll set up UnityEvents to create flexible, designer-friendly callbacks in the Inspector. With UnityEvent, a level designer can wire a button or pickup to any public method without changing code. Fourth, you'll implement basic collision detection using OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter, and establish safe communication between scripts on different GameObjects, including performing null checks before calling another script's methods. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters in a real project, and you'll practice wiring these behaviors in the Inspector so runtime behavior is predictable and maintainable.

To make steady progress, follow a simple learning path. First, learn the syntax and structure of functions, UnityEvent, and the collision callbacks. Practice by writing simple methods and confirming they run. Next, apply those skills by wiring UnityEvent callbacks in the Inspector and by creating small interactions—like a pickup that heals the player via an event or an enemy that takes damage from a function call. Finally, master the patterns by combining them: create reusable damage functions, trigger events on collisions, and use safe script references with null checks and inspector-assigned objects. Along the way, test for common mistakes such as missing Rigidbody components or unassigned references. This progression helps you move from seeing code run to designing interactions that others on your team, such as level designers, can change without touching scripts.

A function, also called a method in C#, is a named block of code that performs a single task and can be called from other places in your scripts. It typically has a return type that says what it gives back after running or void if it returns nothing, a name that communicates purpose, and optionally parameters that accept inputs. For example, a TakeDamage function that accepts an integer amount centralizes health reduction so you never duplicate the logic in many places. A CalculateDistance function can accept two Vector3 positions and return a float distance. Writing functions makes code modular: you can change the logic in one place rather than hunting through many scripts. A common misconception is to think functions should always be short. While readability is important, functions should represent a single logical operation — complex behavior can be composed from smaller functions. This makes testing easier and reduces bugs. In practice, mark functions public when other scripts should call them, and keep utility methods private when they are internal helpers. Consider naming and parameter choices carefully so the function reads like a sentence when called.

Turning repeated logic into a reusable function follows a small process. First, identify the repeated behavior: damage calculation, health clamping, or playing a sound. Second, list the varying inputs: the damage amount, the damage type, or a target GameObject. Third, design the function signature: choose a descriptive name, decide parameters and the return type if needed. Fourth, move the logic into the function body and replace each duplicate with a call. Finally, test all call sites to confirm behavior is unchanged. For example, TakeDamage(int amount) can accept an enum for damage type or return a bool indicating whether the entity died; those choices depend on how callers use the function. A frequent misconception is overloading every small behavior into a single function. Instead, prefer smaller functions that compose into larger behavior. Smaller functions are easier to unit test and reason about. Also document side effects, such as whether the function calls Destroy or triggers animations, so callers know the contract. The result is less duplication and fewer bugs when behavior changes. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

UnityEvent is a Unity system that lets you expose callback points in your scripts so any public method on a GameObject's component can be called when an event fires. You declare a UnityEvent field, for example public UnityEvent OnPlayerCollectedItem, and then call OnPlayerCollectedItem. Invoke() at the appropriate time in your script. In the Inspector, designers can drag GameObjects into the event and pick which public method to call, including methods with parameters that are allowed by UnityEvent. This decouples the code that triggers the event from the concrete objects that respond, which makes interaction wiring flexible and maintainable. A common misconception is to treat UnityEvent as a replacement for all code; instead, use it for designer-configurable connections while keeping important game logic in functions. Another practical tip is to include defensive checks or fallback behavior in case no listeners are assigned. Remember to include using UnityEngine. Events at the top of your C# file to access UnityEvent. In short, UnityEvent moves wiring from code into the Editor so the same trigger can invoke different effects across levels without changing scripts.

To make a UnityEvent work end-to-end, follow a clear sequence. First, add using UnityEngine. Events at the top of your file and declare a public UnityEvent field. Second, in the Inspector, expand the event and use the plus button to add listeners: drag a GameObject into the slot and then choose a public method on one of its components. Third, ensure that the method you want to call is public and matches one of the accepted signatures UnityEvent supports. Fourth, in your script call MyEvent. Invoke() when the condition occurs, for example when the player picks up an item. Fifth, test the scene and confirm that the chosen methods run. A common error is forgetting to mark the method public or selecting a method with an incompatible signature in the Inspector. Unity provides two families of callbacks for interactions: OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter. OnCollisionEnter is used for physical collisions when colliders contact and at least one object has a Rigidbody; it supplies a Collision object with contact information. Use collisions when objects should bounce, push, or respond physically. OnTriggerEnter is used when a collider marked Is Trigger detects overlaps; this does not cause physical responses and is ideal for zones, pickups, or fields. These key concepts are the quick reference you will return to while building interactions. First, functions or methods encapsulate a single task with a clear name, parameters, and possibly a return type; design them to be reusable. Second, the return type declares what a function gives back or void when nothing is returned. Third, parameters let a function operate on different data without duplicating code. Mastering these three ideas helps you keep game logic modular and maintainable. When you write a TakeDamage method, think about what inputs it needs and whether it should return a success flag or simply be void. These final concepts focus on interaction and safety. UnityEvent lets you expose callbacks to the Inspector so designers can wire responses without code changes: declare, bind in the Editor, and Invoke. OnCollisionEnter is for physical contact and provides collision details; OnTriggerEnter is for overlap detection without physics when a collider has Is Trigger checked. Scripts communicate by obtaining references via inspector fields, GetComponent variants, scene searches, or singletons; each approach has trade-offs in performance and coupling. Always perform null checks after obtaining references to prevent NullReferenceException and log helpful warnings or errors in Awake when a critical component is missing. Together these practices make interactions flexible for designers and robust for runtime.
